newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Alcoa unit to fan Deceuninck growth.
newsitem.headline: Alcoa unit to fan Deceuninck growth.

text.p: Belgian polyvinyl chloride profiles producer Deceuninck Plastics Industries NV said on Friday its U.S. prospects had blossomed after the takeover this month of Aluminum Co. of America (Alcoa) unit Dayton Technologies Inc.
"It's a very modern company which has everything it takes to make it on the U.S. market," Deceuninck Chief Executive Officer Clement De Meersman told Reuters after a news conference on 1996 earnings.
Dayton Technologies, based in Monroe, Ohio, is the second largest U.S. company active in the extrusion of plastic door- and window profiles with a 1996 net turnover of $52 million.
Deceuninck said that Dayton Technologies had no debt and minimal goodwill and had tax deductible fixed assets of more than $50 million.
Deceuninck also secured of $8.0 million in tax savings on the Dayton purchase in the next five to eight years.
De Meersman said he expected the turnover of Dayton Technologies, which already grew more than 300 percent since 1989, to rise to $95 million within five years.
Following the 100-percent takeover of Dayton, Deceuninck said consolidated turnover was most likely to exceed $230 million in 1997.
Deceuninck was already active on the northern American market through Slocomb Industries which it acquired in 1995. Combined U.S. sales are expected to top $100 million by the turn of the century.
De Meersman added he expected equally strong growth in East and Central Europe for Deceuninck, which is planning to build a PVC profiles plant near the Polish city of Poznan.
It is also opening a sales office in Russia.
De Meersman told the news conference that Deceuninck was keeping a close eye on Russia and was ready "to take off" once that market started developing.
"But for now growth is mainly in other countries," he said.
He noted that the German construction sector remained very weak and was hoping for a revival there "so that our German colleagues would focus more on their own market".
France saw a decline in overall building activities but the PVC market held steady. Business in the Benelux countries were also stable and Britain showed an upturn.

Deceuninck had a 29.6 percent rise in 1996 consolidated net profit to 464 million francs and De Meersman said earnings were also developing well in the first few months of 1997 with sales up seven to eight percent.
"1996 has been a very good year indeed," he said.
Deceuninck plans to pay a net dividend per share of 59 francs, up a modest five percent.
"We're trying to keep some money in the company because we have an ambitious growth strategy and also keep an eye on East Europe," De Meersman said.
He declined to comment on any new investments for 1997, adding those would be announced at the company's shareholders meeting in May.
De Meersman said he expected PVC prices to climb further
"But they will not jump," he added. "There is enough PVC available". -- Brussels Newsroom, +32 2 287 6815
